walkthroughs.body_html:
Practical Skills — a core area of A-Level Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Practical Skills brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Practical Skills.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a control variable in an enzyme experiment?
options: pH
Rate of reaction
Independent variable
Time taken

mcqs.q: Which direction does water move in the xylem, and what drives it?
options: Water moves both directions in the xylem depending on the time of day.
Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.
Upwards from roots to leaves — driven mainly by transpiration pull (evaporation at leaves creating tension on the water column).
Water moves up the xylem because roots pump it actively using ATP.

mcqs.q: How does myelination increase the speed of nerve impulse conduction?
options: Myelin makes the axon thicker so the signal travels faster through more material.
Water moves both directions in the xylem depending on the time of day.
Action potentials jump between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), skipping the myelinated sections.
Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.

mcqs.q: What reads the mRNA codons during translation?
options: tRNA molecules carrying specific amino acids — their anticodons pair with mRNA codons at the ribosome.
DNA directly reads the codons on mRNA and adds amino acids.
Ribosomes synthesise amino acids from scratch using the mRNA as a template.
Myelin contains additional ion channels that speed up depolarisation.
